Technical Case: Failure Analysis in an FPSO¶

Dataset¶

The dataset contains anonymized time series records of a machine's operation from an FPSO (Floating Production Storage and Offloading).

Recorded Variables¶

The recorded variables are as follows:

  • Cycle: Sequential identifier of measurement cycles.
  • Preset_1 & Preset_2: Variables that control a specific operating point of the machine.
  • Temperature: Temperature recorded in the equipment.
  • Vibrations (X, Y & Z): Vibrations along the machine's axes.
  • Frequency: Operating frequency of the machine.
  • Fail: Variable indicating whether the machine is in a failure state at the given timestamp.

Tasks¶

Note: During the FPSO’s operation, various factors can cause the machine to fail and prolong its failure state. Explore the available data, identify, and calculate the metrics required below.

1. Calculate how many times the equipment has failed¶

2. Categorize equipment failures by setup configurations (Preset 1 and Preset 2)¶

3. Categorize equipment failures by their nature/root cause¶

4. Create a model (or models) and measure its performance¶

5. Analyze variable importance¶

# Numeric outliers by the IQR rule, flagged by machine state

def iqr_outliers(series):
    q1, q3 = series.quantile(0.25), series.quantile(0.75)
    iqr = q3 - q1
    lower, upper = q1 - 1.5 * iqr, q3 + 1.5 * iqr
    mask = (series < lower) | (series > upper)
    return mask, lower, upper

for col in sensors:
    mask, lower, upper = iqr_outliers(df[col])
    out = df.loc[mask, [col, "Fail"]]
    n = len(out)
    n_fail = int(out["Fail"].sum())
    print(f"{col}: {n} outliers (bounds: {lower:.1f} / {upper:.1f}) "
          f"| {n_fail} in failure, {n - n_fail} in operation")

Initial Findings
  • There are 800 instances in the dataset.
  • There are no missing values (every feature has 800 observations).
  • Target variable (Fail) is binary.
  • Class imbalance: failure rows represent 8.25% of observations (91.75% vs. 8.25%). This is a per-row rate; because failures persist across consecutive cycles, the number of distinct failure events is much smaller. The effective imbalance for modeling will depend on how the prediction target is defined (see Target Definition in Task 4 approach).
  • Outlier values cannot be directly associated with failures, since most outliers fall in the operating (non-failure) category. To find a reliable failure signal we likely need to look at the operating regimes (presets) and at the sensor values in the n cycles preceding each failure.
  • Across all sensors, the failure-state distributions are shifted toward higher values relative to normal operation, but they overlap heavily with the operating distributions: most high values still occur during normal operation. A single-sensor threshold therefore cannot separate the classes, this overlap is what motivates a multivariate and/or temporal approach.
  • Sensor-to-sensor correlations are low to moderate (max ~0.58), with no pair high enough to indicate redundancy, so no sensor is dropped on that basis. Spearman exceeds Pearson across most pairs, suggesting monotonic but non-linear relationships, which favors models able to capture non-linearity.

Task 1¶

  1. Calculate how many times the equipment has failed. During the FPSO’s operation, various factors can cause the machine to fail and prolong its failure state. We ask you to explore the available data, identify, and calculate the number of times the equipment has failed throughout its operation.
  • Transform each fail True to 1 and False to 0.
  • Compute diff to previous row to detect the transition of the state of the machine, this will result in 3 outputs:
    • 0 -> no changes in the state of the machine,
    • 1 -> failure starts,
    • -1 -> machine recovery
  • failure_starts = True for output == 1, False otherwise (0 or -1)
  • Sum all of the time a failure starts
  • Handle the edge case where the machine starts in failure mode: failure_starts.iloc[0] = (fail.iloc[0] == 1)

In [309]:
# Inspect how the presets behave over time and whether failures align with any preset pattern.
# Two diagnostic questions:
#   1. Do presets form plateaus (stable regime for many cycles) or a sawtooth (changing every cycle)?
#   2. Do failures (red points) concentrate at a particular preset level or transition?
# The series is split into 200-cycle chunks for readability (800 cycles in one axis is unreadable),
# and Preset_1 / Preset_2 are plotted separately because their scales differ (3 vs 8 levels).

fail_mask = df["Fail"].values
chunk_size = 200
n_chunks = int(np.ceil(len(df) / chunk_size))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(n_chunks * 2, 1, figsize=(15, 3 * n_chunks * 2))
for i in range(n_chunks):
    lo, hi = i * chunk_size, (i + 1) * chunk_size
    seg = df.iloc[lo:hi]
    seg_fail = seg[seg["Fail"]]

    ax1 = axes[i * 2]
    ax1.plot(seg["Cycle"], seg["Preset_1"], marker=".", linewidth=0.5)
    ax1.scatter(seg_fail["Cycle"], seg_fail["Preset_1"], color="red", zorder=5, s=40, label="Fail")
    ax1.set_ylabel(f"Preset_1\n({lo}-{hi})")
    ax1.legend(loc="upper right")

    ax2 = axes[i * 2 + 1]
    ax2.plot(seg["Cycle"], seg["Preset_2"], marker=".", linewidth=0.5, color="tab:orange")
    ax2.scatter(seg_fail["Cycle"], seg_fail["Preset_2"], color="red", zorder=5, s=40, label="Fail")
    ax2.set_ylabel(f"Preset_2\n({lo}-{hi})")
    ax2.legend(loc="upper right")

axes[-1].set_xlabel("Cycle")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Task 2 answer¶

  • Sawtooth behavior. Preset_1 and Preset_2 change every cycle, showing no plateau or prolonged regime, they act as an instantaneous operating condition, not as extended operating phases. No regime shift is observed prior to failure.
  • Failures categorized by configuration (two complementary lenses). Per-row (marginal tables): the share of time spent in failure under each preset level. Per-event (df[failure_starts]): the configuration active at the moment each failure was triggered. Both are reported because they answer different questions; they converge on the same conclusion.
  • Per-event view is too sparse for conclusions. The 10 failure events are scattered across 9 of the 24 possible Preset_1×Preset_2 combinations, with at most 2 per cell. With 10 events over 24 cells, a count of 2 in a single cell is expected by chance and does not indicate a higher-risk configuration.
  • Preset_1 marginal: level 1 shows a slightly higher failure rate (~10% vs. ~7%), but the difference is weak and likely within sampling noise.
  • Preset_2 marginal: failure rates range from ~3% to ~12% across its 8 levels, but this compares post-hoc extremes over many levels with ~100 samples each; the gap is roughly 2 standard errors and is compatible with sampling noise. No single level is reliably more failure-prone.

Taken together, the failure signal is not in the instantaneous operating configuration, neither in individual presets nor in their combination. This motivates the temporal analysis that follows: the signal is likely in the dynamics, i.e. how sensor values evolve in the cycles preceding a failure.

Task 3¶

  1. Categorize equipment failures by their nature/root cause according to parameter readings (temperature, pressure, and others). Analyze patterns in these readings that could indicate specific failure types. How do these patterns differ across operational regimes? Provide insights based on your findings.
In [310]:
sensors = ["Temperature", "Pressure", "VibrationX", "VibrationY", "VibrationZ", "Frequency"]

# Reference statistics computed on NORMAL operation only, to avoid letting
# failure values contaminate the definition of "normal".
normal = df[~df["Fail"]]

# Global z-score: how far each value is from the overall normal baseline
for s in sensors:
    mu, sigma = normal[s].mean(), normal[s].std()
    df[f"{s}_z"] = (df[s] - mu) / sigma

# Per-regime z-score: "normal" defined within each Preset_1 level
# Uses transform so each row is standardized against its own regime's normal stats.
normal_stats = normal.groupby("Preset_1")[sensors].agg(["mean", "std"])

for s in sensors:
    # map each row's regime to that regime's normal mean/std
    mu = df["Preset_1"].map(normal_stats[(s, "mean")])
    sigma = df["Preset_1"].map(normal_stats[(s, "std")])
    df[f"{s}_z_regime"] = (df[s] - mu) / sigma
In [311]:
# Sanity-check the per-regime z-score denominators: each sensor's normal std
# should be similar across Preset_1 levels. A collapsed/near-zero std in one
# regime would inflate that regime's z-scores and create false extremes.

sigmas = normal.groupby("Preset_1")[sensors].std()
sigmas.round(2).reset_index()

Operating regime does not modulate sensor behavior

Standardizing each sensor against the global normal baseline and against each regime's own normal baseline produces nearly identical z-scores for Preset_1: the mean absolute difference per sensor is only ~0.05–0.07 SD (max ~0.7 SD in isolated points), with no collapsed or inflated per-regime denominators. This indicates the normal behavior of the sensors does not depend on the Preset_1 regime.

For Preset_2 the differences are somewhat larger (mean abs diff ~0.07–0.16 SD, highest for Temperature). However, Preset_2 has 8 levels with only ~90 normal samples each, versus ~240 per level for Preset_1's 3 levels, so its per-level mean/std estimates are less stable. These larger differences are plausibly estimation noise from the smaller per-level sample rather than genuine modulation; the data cannot distinguish the two at this sample size. We therefore treat the Preset_1 result as robust and the Preset_2 result as inconclusive.

Either way, the effect is modest, so we analyze failure signatures globally rather than slicing the 10 events across regimes (which would be too sparse to support conclusions). We proceed with the global z-score.

In [314]:

# z=2 is the standard statistical anomaly threshold: in a roughly-normal distribution,
# |z| > 2 lies beyond ~2 SD and covers only ~2.3% of the tail. We START from this
# theoretical value, then VALIDATE it empirically here by comparing how often each
# sensor exceeds it during NORMAL operation vs during FAILURE.
# The contrast (not the normal fraction alone) is what matters:
# - The normal fraction is partly circular (z-scores were standardized on normal data,
#   so ~2-3% above 2 is expected by construction).
# - The failure fraction is the genuine signal: it was NOT used to build the z-scores,
#   so a much higher rate there shows z>2 discriminates between states rather than
#   flagging routine fluctuation.

z_cols = [f"{s}_z" for s in sensors]

THRESHOLD = 2.0

normal_rows = df[~df["Fail"]]
fail_rows = df[df["Fail"]]

print(f"Fraction of points with z > {THRESHOLD} (per sensor):\n")
print(f"{'Sensor':<14}{'Normal':>10}{'Failure':>10}")
for s, zc in zip(sensors, z_cols):
    frac_normal = (normal_rows[zc] > THRESHOLD).mean()
    frac_fail = (fail_rows[zc] > THRESHOLD).mean()
    print(f"{s:<14}{frac_normal:>10.3%}{frac_fail:>10.3%}")

all_normal = (normal_rows[z_cols] > THRESHOLD).values.mean()
all_fail = (fail_rows[z_cols] > THRESHOLD).values.mean()
print(f"\nOverall: {all_normal:.3%} of normal sensor-readings vs {all_fail:.3%} of failure sensor-readings exceed z={THRESHOLD}")

The z=2 threshold is anchored both theoretically (≈2 SD from normal behavior) and empirically: only 3.2% of normal-operation sensor readings exceed it, versus 21.5% during failure (≈7× higher), confirming it discriminates between normal and failure states rather than flagging routine fluctuation.

Pre-failure window choice (5 cycles)

The pre-failure window is set to 5 cycles. Comparing 3- vs 5-cycle windows showed that some episodes (e.g. onset 13) exhibit precursor signals only 4–5 cycles before failure, which a 3-cycle window misses entirely. Capturing these justifies the longer window.

The trade-off: for the three most closely-spaced episodes (minimum inter-episode gap = 4 cycles), the 5-cycle window may include 1–2 cycles of the preceding episode, a limitation we note explicitly, inherent to the event proximity in this dataset.

Task 3 Answer¶

Task 3 — Failure categorization by sensor signature
  • Regime does not materially change patterns. Sensor behavior standardized per operating regime is nearly identical to the global baseline (robust for Preset_1; inconclusive but modest for Preset_2 due to small per-level samples). So failure signatures are analyzed globally rather than sliced by regime.
  • Failures are heterogeneous. Using a z > 2 anomaly threshold (z > 2 occurs in only 3.2% of normal readings vs 21.5% during failure, ~7×), the pre-failure signature varies across episodes: some are thermal (Temperature/Frequency), others vibrational on different axes (VibrationX, Y, or Z), and others mixed. There is no single shared failure signature.
  • Candidate failure types (tentative): thermal (onsets 157, 263, 550), vibrational (13, 270, 415, 700, 793), and no-clear-precursor / near-sudden (163, 538). These are exploratory groupings, not validated types.
  • Precursor ≠ onset signature. The sensors anomalous in the cycles before failure generally differ from those anomalous at onset (e.g. onset 263: Temperature precursor, no clear onset signal). This is partly a measurement artifact (precursor = peak over 5 cycles vs onset = single cycle), but it also indicates that pre-failure dynamics carry information the instantaneous value does not, supporting the use of windowed/temporal features in the model (Task 4).

Caveat: with only 10 failure events, any typification rests on 2–3 episodes per group and cannot be statistically validated. Inter-episode contamination (minimum gap = 4 cycles) also adds noise to precursor measurement. The typology should be read as an exploratory hypothesis for investigation with more data, not a confirmed taxonomy.

Task 4¶

Task 4 — Approach

Problem framing. The goal is to predict failure before it occurs, so this is not detection of the current state but classification of an upcoming event: "will the machine fail within the next τ cycles?" We build this lookahead target and drop in-failure rows from training,we predict the onset, not the continuation of an ongoing failure. This is also supported by Task 3, where the sensors anomalous during failure differ from the precursor signal.

Lookahead horizon (τ = 5). τ is set from the pre-failure analysis, which showed precursor signals concentrated in the ~1–5 cycles before onset (with reliable early warnings up to 5 cycles ahead in the analyzable episodes). It is chosen from the data, not tuned on the test metric. τ = 3 is also evaluated as a sensitivity check.

Features. Raw sensors plus backward-looking rolling statistics (mean, std over 3 and 5 cycles). These are motivated by Task 3, which showed that pre-failure dynamics carry signal the instantaneous reading does not. Window sizes match the precursor scale.

Validation and metrics. Splits are strictly temporal (train on the past, test on the future) to avoid leakage. PR-AUC is the primary metric, since accuracy is meaningless under ~7% positives. Class imbalance is handled with cost-sensitive class weighting rather than resampling, to preserve the temporal structure.

Models. We progress from simple to complex — logistic regression (linear baseline), gradient boosting (non-linear), and Isolation Forest (unsupervised anomaly detection), adopting more complexity only if it earns its place. With only 10 failure events, all choices favor simplicity and regularization over capacity.

Data Prep¶

In [319]:
def create_target(df: pd.DataFrame, tau: int, fail_col: str = "Fail") -> pd.Series:
    """Build a predictive-maintenance target: will the machine fail within the next 'tau' cycles?

    For each row at cycle t, the target is 1 if a failure occurs in the window
    (t, t + tau], i.e. in any of the next 'tau' cycles, and 0 otherwise.

    Rows that are already in a failure state are excluded from being positive
    targets (we predict the onset of failure, not its continuation): the caller
    should decide whether to drop in-failure rows before training.

    Args:
        df: DataFrame sorted by cycle, containing a boolean failure column.
        tau: Lookahead horizon in cycles (must be >= 1).
        fail_col: Name of the boolean failure column.

    Returns:
        Int Series (0/1) aligned to df.index: 1 if failure occurs within the
        next 'tau' cycles, else 0.
    """
    if tau < 1:
        raise ValueError(f"tau must be >= 1, got {tau}")

    fail = df[fail_col].astype(int).to_numpy()
    n = len(fail)
    target = np.zeros(n, dtype=int)

    for i in range(n):
        # look at the next tau cycles: positions i+1 .. i+tau
        window = fail[i + 1 : i + 1 + tau]
        if window.sum() > 0:
            target[i] = 1

    return pd.Series(target, index=df.index, name=f"will_fail_within_{tau}")
In [320]:
def add_window_features(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    sensors: list[str],
    windows: tuple[int, ...] = (3, 5),
    stats: tuple[str, ...] = ("mean", "std"),
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Add backward-looking rolling-window features for each sensor.

    For each sensor and window size, computes rolling statistics over the
    current and preceding 'w - 1' cycles (trailing window, never centered),
    so no future information leaks into a row's features.

    Args:
        df: DataFrame sorted by cycle.
        sensors: Sensor column names to compute features for.
        windows: Rolling window sizes in cycles.
        stats: Statistics to compute ('mean', 'std').

    Returns:
        A copy of df with added feature columns named '{sensor}_{stat}_{w}'.
    """
    out = df.copy()
    for sensor in sensors:
        for w in windows:
            roll = out[sensor].rolling(window=w, min_periods=1)
            for stat in stats:
                out[f"{sensor}_{stat}_{w}"] = getattr(roll, stat)()
    return out
In [321]:
def temporal_split(df: pd.DataFrame, cycle_col: str = "Cycle", test_ratio: float = 0.2) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, pd.DataFrame]:
    """Split chronologically: earliest (1 - test_ratio) cycles for train, latest for test.

    No shuffling: train always precedes test in time, preventing temporal leakage.

    Args:
        df: DataFrame sorted by cycle.
        cycle_col: Name of the cycle column.
        test_ratio: Fraction of the time span held out as the most recent test set.

    Returns:
        (train_df, test_df) split at the temporal cutoff.
    """
    cutoff = df[cycle_col].quantile(1 - test_ratio)
    train = df[df[cycle_col] <= cutoff].copy()
    test = df[df[cycle_col] > cutoff].copy()
    return train, test
In [322]:
def prepare_data(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    sensors: list[str],
    tau: int,
    windows: tuple[int, ...] = (3, 5),
    test_ratio: float = 0.2,
) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, pd.DataFrame, pd.Series, pd.Series, list[str]]:
    """End-to-end preprocessing for the predictive-maintenance task.

    Steps:
        1. Build the lookahead target on the full series.
        2. Add backward-looking window features on the full series (needs temporal continuity).
        3. Drop in-failure rows (we predict onset, not continuation).
        4. Temporal train/test split (no shuffle).
        5. Fit the scaler on train only, transform both.

    Args:
        df: Raw DataFrame sorted by cycle.
        sensors: Sensor column names.
        tau: Lookahead horizon in cycles.
        windows: Rolling window sizes.
        test_ratio: Most-recent fraction held out for testing.

    Returns:
        (X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test, feature_cols), scaled and ready to fit a model.
    """
    work = df.sort_values("Cycle").reset_index(drop=True).copy()

    # (1) target on the full series
    work["target"] = create_target(work, tau=tau)

    # (2) window features on the full series (backward-looking, no leakage)
    work = add_window_features(work, sensors=sensors, windows=windows)

    # (3) drop in-failure rows: predict the onset, not the failure state itself
    work = work[~work["Fail"]].copy()

    # feature columns: raw sensors + window features (exclude target, Fail, Cycle, presets)
    window_cols = [f"{s}_{stat}_{w}" for s in sensors for w in windows for stat in ("mean", "std")]
    feature_cols = sensors + window_cols

    # (4) temporal split
    train, test = temporal_split(work, test_ratio=test_ratio)

    # (5) fit scaler on train only, transform both
    scaler = StandardScaler()
    X_train = pd.DataFrame(
        scaler.fit_transform(train[feature_cols]),
        columns=feature_cols, index=train.index,
    )
    X_test = pd.DataFrame(
        scaler.transform(test[feature_cols]),
        columns=feature_cols, index=test.index,
    )
    y_train = train["target"]
    y_test = test["target"]

    return X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test, feature_cols

Why a single train/test split fails here, and why we move to forward-chaining CV

The baseline models (logistic regression: PR-AUC 0.072; gradient boosting: 0.119) performed near the random baseline (~0.07 for a 7% positive rate). Before concluding the precursor signal is too weak, we checked how the temporal split distributes the failure events.

The test set has only 2 onsets. With a single 80/20 temporal cut, 8 of the 10 failure onsets fall in training and only 2 in test. Evaluating failure prediction on 2 events is not statistically meaningful, any test metric is dominated by sampling noise. The poor scores are therefore uninformative, not evidence that prediction is impossible.

Root cause: with only 10 failure events, any single split leaves the test side with too few events to evaluate. This is a fundamental consequence of event scarcity.

Solution: forward-chaining (time-series) cross-validation, multiple progressive cuts, always training on the past and testing on the future, so events are distributed across test folds. We aggregate metrics across folds and report their spread, and use the same structure to test lookahead sensitivity (τ = 3, 5, 10). Expectation: even so, 10 events yield high variance, this remains a proof of concept, not a production model.

In [281]:
def evaluate_cv(df: pd.DataFrame, sensors: list[str], tau: int,
                n_splits: int = 3, windows: tuple[int, ...] = (3, 5)) -> dict:
    """Forward-chaining CV for a given tau. Returns per-fold PR-AUC for both models.

    Builds target + window features on the full series, drops in-failure rows,
    then applies TimeSeriesSplit. Scaler is fit on each training fold only.
    Folds with no positives in the test split yield NaN (PR-AUC undefined).
    """
    work = df.sort_values("Cycle").reset_index(drop=True).copy()
    work["target"] = create_target(work, tau=tau)
    work = add_window_features(work, sensors=sensors, windows=windows)
    work = work[~work["Fail"]].reset_index(drop=True)

    window_cols = [f"{s}_{stat}_{w}" for s in sensors for w in windows for stat in ("mean", "std")]
    feature_cols = sensors + window_cols
    X_all = work[feature_cols].fillna(0)
    y_all = work["target"]

    tscv = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=n_splits)
    results = {"logreg": [], "gb": [], "test_positives": []}

    for tr_idx, te_idx in tscv.split(X_all):
        X_tr, X_te = X_all.iloc[tr_idx], X_all.iloc[te_idx]
        y_tr, y_te = y_all.iloc[tr_idx], y_all.iloc[te_idx]
        results["test_positives"].append(int(y_te.sum()))

        if y_te.sum() == 0 or y_tr.sum() == 0:
            results["logreg"].append(np.nan)
            results["gb"].append(np.nan)
            continue

        scaler = StandardScaler()
        X_tr_s = scaler.fit_transform(X_tr)
        X_te_s = scaler.transform(X_te)

        lr = LogisticRegression(class_weight="balanced", max_iter=1000, random_state=42)
        lr.fit(X_tr_s, y_tr)
        results["logreg"].append(average_precision_score(y_te, lr.predict_proba(X_te_s)[:, 1]))

        pw = (y_tr == 0).sum() / (y_tr == 1).sum()
        sw = y_tr.map({0: 1.0, 1: pw})
        gb = HistGradientBoostingClassifier(max_depth=3, learning_rate=0.05, max_iter=200,
                                            l2_regularization=1.0, random_state=42)
        gb.fit(X_tr_s, y_tr, sample_weight=sw)
        results["gb"].append(average_precision_score(y_te, gb.predict_proba(X_te_s)[:, 1]))

    return results


for tau in (3, 5, 10):
    res = evaluate_cv(df, sensors, tau=tau)
    lr_scores = [x for x in res["logreg"] if not np.isnan(x)]
    gb_scores = [x for x in res["gb"] if not np.isnan(x)]
    print(f"\nτ={tau} | test positives per fold: {res['test_positives']}")
    print(f"  LogReg PR-AUC per fold: {[round(x,3) if not np.isnan(x) else None for x in res['logreg']]}")
    print(f"  GB     PR-AUC per fold: {[round(x,3) if not np.isnan(x) else None for x in res['gb']]}")
    if lr_scores:
        print(f"  Mean — LogReg: {np.mean(lr_scores):.3f} | GB: {np.mean(gb_scores):.3f} (over {len(lr_scores)} valid folds)")

Why test an unsupervised anomaly detector (Isolation Forest)?

The supervised models must learn from only 10 failure events, the core limitation. Isolation Forest takes a different angle: it trains only on normal-operation data (abundant, ~700 rows), learns the boundary of normal behavior, and flags deviations as anomalies. It needs no failure examples to train, so it addresses the scarcity of positives by a fundamentally different paradigm.

Testing a distinct paradigm also makes the conclusion more robust: if a non-supervised method hits the same performance ceiling as the supervised ones, the limit is the signal in the data, not the choice of model family.

Caveat: anomaly detection flags a deviation when it occurs, so it tends to fire close to the failure onset, i.e. detection is often late, with little lead time. This is a known limitation for prediction: it works well only if the precursor is anomalous enough, far enough ahead. Given the pre-failure analysis (signal concentrated near −1), we expect limited foresight here.

To keep the comparison fair and aligned with prediction (not detection), we use the same setup as the classifiers: in-failure rows are dropped, the positive target is the pre-failure window, and we train only on pure-normal rows (excluding both failures and the pre-failure window) so the detector does not learn precursor patterns as "normal".

In [270]:
def evaluate_isolation_forest(df, sensors, tau, n_splits=3, windows=(3, 5),
                              prefail_exclude=5):
    """Anomaly detection, aligned with the classifier setup: in-failure rows are
    dropped from the whole dataset (we predict onset, not detect ongoing failure).
    Train on pure-normal rows; positives are the pre-failure window only.
    """
    work = df.sort_values("Cycle").reset_index(drop=True).copy()
    work["target"] = create_target(work, tau=tau)
    work = add_window_features(work, sensors=sensors, windows=windows)
    work["in_prefail"] = create_target(work, tau=prefail_exclude).astype(bool)

    # drop in-failure rows from EVERYTHING (same as the classifier)
    work = work[~work["Fail"]].reset_index(drop=True)
    work["pure_normal"] = ~work["in_prefail"]

    window_cols = [f"{s}_{stat}_{w}" for s in sensors for w in windows for stat in ("mean", "std")]
    feature_cols = sensors + window_cols
    work[feature_cols] = work[feature_cols].fillna(0)

    X_all, y_all, pure = work[feature_cols], work["target"], work["pure_normal"]
    tscv = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=n_splits)
    scores, pos_per_fold = [], []

    for tr_idx, te_idx in tscv.split(X_all):
        tr_mask = work.index.isin(tr_idx) & pure
        y_te = y_all.iloc[te_idx]
        pos_per_fold.append(int(y_te.sum()))

        if tr_mask.sum() < 20 or y_te.sum() == 0:
            scores.append(np.nan)
            continue

        scaler = StandardScaler().fit(X_all[tr_mask])
        iso = IsolationForest(n_estimators=200, contamination="auto", random_state=42)
        iso.fit(scaler.transform(X_all[tr_mask]))
        anomaly_score = -iso.score_samples(scaler.transform(X_all.iloc[te_idx]))
        scores.append(average_precision_score(y_te, anomaly_score))

    valid = [s for s in scores if not np.isnan(s)]
    return scores, valid, pos_per_fold


for tau in (3, 5, 10):
    scores, valid, pos = evaluate_isolation_forest(df, sensors, tau=tau)
    print(f"\nτ={tau} | test positives per fold: {pos}")
    print(f"  IF PR-AUC per fold: {[round(s,3) if not np.isnan(s) else None for s in scores]}")
    if valid:
        print(f"  Mean: {np.mean(valid):.3f} ({len(valid)} valid folds)")

Task 4 Answer¶

Task 4 — Model and performance
  • Target formulation. Predicting failure before it occurs is framed as binary classification: "will the machine fail within the next τ cycles?" In-failure rows are dropped (we predict onset, not continuation; their onset signature also differs from the precursor, see Task 3). τ = 5 is justified by the pre-failure analysis (precursor concentrated in the ~5 cycles before onset), with τ = 3 and 10 tested for sensitivity.
  • Features. Raw sensors plus backward-looking rolling statistics (mean, std over 3 and 5 cycles), motivated by Task 3 showing pre-failure dynamics carry signal the instantaneous value does not. Window sizes match the precursor scale, not τ.
  • Validation. A single 80/20 temporal split placed only 2 of 10 onsets in test, too few to evaluate. We use forward-chaining (TimeSeriesSplit, 3 folds) CV instead, training on the past and testing on the future, with PR-AUC as the primary metric (accuracy is meaningless at ~7% positives). Class imbalance handled via cost-sensitive weighting (no resampling, to preserve temporal structure).
  • Three methods converge on the same ceiling. Logistic regression (linear), gradient boosting (non-linear), and Isolation Forest (unsupervised anomaly detection) all land in mean PR-AUC ≈ 0.1–0.25, above the ~0.07 random baseline (signal exists), but far from deployable. Gradient boosting is consistently ≥ logistic regression, giving modest support to non-linearity mattering. Notably, the same middle fold scores highest across all three methods, indicating the variation is driven by which period falls in the test fold, not by the model.
  • Key diagnostic. Since three very different paradigms hit the same limit, the bottleneck is the signal in the data, not the model choice or features. The precursor is weak until ~1 cycle before onset (Task 3), so short-horizon prediction is intrinsically hard here.

Caveat: with only 10 failure events, per-fold metrics have high variance and τ comparisons are not conclusive, the higher mean at τ = 10 comes from a single lucky fold, not genuinely better foresight (its other folds stay in the same low range). This is a proof of concept demonstrating detectable but insufficient signal, not a production model. The dominant limitation is event scarcity; more failure events are the prerequisite for a deployable model.

Task 5¶

Task 5 - Reading variable importance with caution

Variable importance answers "which features did the model rely on most", but for a model that only reaches PR-AUC ≈ 0.2, that is the importance of a weak model. It reflects what this limited model used, not necessarily what physically drives failure. With only 10 events, the ranking is indicative, not definitive: it will shift with the fold, the seed, and the method.

Mitigation: cross-check multiple methods. We do not rely on a single importance measure. We combine permutation importance (impact on the actual metric, model-agnostic) with SHAP (per-prediction contributions, with direction). If the methods agree, the conclusion is more robust despite each one's fragility; if they disagree, that disagreement is itself a finding consistent with the weak signal.

Correlated-feature caveat. The vibration axes are moderately correlated, and a sensor's raw value, rolling mean, and rolling std are correlated with each other. Importance can therefore be diluted across redundant features, and indeed the vibration contribution appears spread thinly across several columns (VibrationX, VibrationZ, in both raw and rolling forms) rather than concentrated, which keeps any single vibration feature low in the ranking.

In [282]:

However, permutation importance points instead to Frequency_mean_5 as the single clearly-above-noise predictor, with vibration features contributing only weakly and diffusely. This partial mismatch is exactly why we cross-check with SHAP below, and why the ranking should be read as suggestive, not conclusive.

Task 5 Answer¶

Task 5 — Variable importance
  • Method. Importance is assessed two ways: permutation importance (drop in PR-AUC when a feature is shuffled, impact on the actual metric) and SHAP (per-prediction contributions). Using two independent methods guards against the fragility of any single measure on a weak model.
  • Top predictor, confirmed by both methods. Frequency_mean_5 (mean frequency over the last 5 cycles) is the single most important feature in both permutation importance (0.041 PR-AUC drop, ~6× its std, the only feature clearly above noise) and SHAP (mean |SHAP| 0.82, well ahead of the next at 0.43). The agreement gives confidence in this finding despite the weak model.
  • Secondary contributors. SHAP shows the next tier dominated by window-5 means of other sensors (VibrationZ, VibrationY, Temperature, VibrationX). This suggests the model relies on the recent smoothed level of the sensors (5-cycle mean) rather than instantaneous values or short-term variability, consistent with the τ = 5 horizon.
  • Vibration is diluted, not absent. The exploratory analyses (Task 3) highlighted vibration, but here vibration importance is spread thinly across axes and forms (raw / mean / std) and never concentrated, exactly the correlated-feature dilution anticipated. Univariate analysis (Task 3) flags vibration because it looks at sensors in isolation; multivariate importance (this task), accounting for the full feature set, elevates frequency instead.
  • Method note. Permutation importance concentrated nearly all importance in one feature (shuffling others barely moved the already-low PR-AUC), while SHAP distributed it more smoothly. The two agree on the leader but differ on the tail, expected, since the metrics measure different things. The leader is robust; the tail ranking is not.

Caveat: this is the importance of a model at PR-AUC ≈ 0.2, indicative of what the model uses, not a validated account of physical failure drivers. With 10 events, the ranking below the top feature is noisy and seed/fold-dependent. The robust takeaway is narrow: short-term mean frequency is the most consistent signal; everything else contributes weakly.

Conclusion and Next Steps: A Literature Supported Approach¶

Literature-informed approach. The modeling and feature-engineering decisions were informed by Al-Ali & Alharbi (2026), "Temporally Rigorous and Traceable Predictive Maintenance via Joint Labeler-Model Optimization." The paper frames predictive maintenance as predicting failure within a lookahead window (τ) rather than detecting it at the moment it occurs, and it emphasizes strict temporal validation. Both ideas were adopted here.

Note on the source: the article is an unedited "in press" manuscript. Its own disclaimer states it is provided for early access, will undergo further editing, and may contain errors. It was therefore used as methodological inspiration rather than as a settled reference.

Adaptations to this dataset. The paper co-optimizes τ and model hyperparameters via Optuna over 876,100 samples and 761 failures. Our dataset has 800 cycles and only 10 failure events, three orders of magnitude fewer. We therefore deliberately did not replicate the automated search, which would overfit on 10 events. Instead we fixed τ = 5 from the pre-failure analysis (precursor concentrated in the roughly 5 cycles before onset), used backward-looking rolling features, enforced temporal validation (forward-chaining CV), and reported PR-AUC rather than accuracy.

Main findings. Three different paradigms (logistic regression, gradient boosting, and Isolation Forest) converged on the same modest ceiling (PR-AUC around 0.1 to 0.25, above the 0.07 random baseline). Because methods this different reach the same limit, the bottleneck is the signal in the data, not the model choice. Variable importance (permutation and SHAP, in agreement) identified short-term mean frequency as the most consistent predictor. This was notably not vibration, which the univariate exploration had suggested, illustrating how multivariate importance can differ from single-sensor analysis.

Assessment. This is a proof of concept that demonstrates detectable but insufficient predictive signal, not a deployable model. The low PR-AUC reflects genuine difficulty, namely a weak precursor (signal emerges only about 1 cycle before onset) compounded by extreme event scarcity, rather than a coding artifact. The absence of inflated metrics is consistent with the leakage-free temporal validation. The dominant limitation is the number of failure events.

Next steps. The pipeline (windowed target, rolling features, temporal CV) is sound and reusable. The prerequisite for a deployable model is more failure history. With more mapped failure events, the same architecture could be re-evaluated, and the automated τ and hyperparameter co-optimization from the paper would become viable. Whether prediction can reach high performance depends on whether the precursor signal strengthens with more data, which remains an open question rather than a guarantee.
